comment: Credit where it is due: putting the NCI registry at rank 2 serves prefers_trials now, while the patient is NED and there is nothing measurable to enroll on. But at recurrence you sequence the trial route below sunitinib and regorafenib, and a patient whose stated preference is trials wants that menu offered co-equal with sunitinib, not after two guideline TKIs. Worth saying too that prefers_trials was defaulted here, not elicited, so I would confirm it before it carries this much ordering weight.

Bundling the NCI registry into rank 1 is the right instinct, it honors prefers_trials while the patient is NED, and your call to run the SDHB re-cut now is exactly what keeps trial eligibility from lapsing. Where we part is the recurrence ladder: ranking sunitinib ahead of the trial agents optimizes for the toxicity you can predict, but the stated preference is trials, so the trial route belongs alongside sunitinib rather than behind it. With no toxicity vetoes on file, the predictability premium buys this patient less than it would a tox-averse one.

This is the pick that protects the patient's trial preference, and I want it on record as such. SDHB reading intact against biallelic SDHA would quietly disqualify this patient at screening for every dSDH contingency trial, so getting the re-cut done now is what keeps prefers_trials from becoming a dead letter at first recurrence. One tissue pull, no therapeutic toxicity, and it guards the eligibility the patient says they want.

Your hold on active therapy now is right for an NED patient and I am glad it is explicit, dosing FGFR or TKI toxicity into someone with no measurable target would be harm for nothing. But ranking rogaratinib first when its trial is closed to accrual and access means compassionate use under-serves a patient whose actual preference is trials; the recruiting in-subtype pemigatinib study at your rank 2 is the one that cashes prefers_trials. Lead with the door that opens.

Advocate presents the trial menu as co-equal with sunitinib at first recurrence, but NCCN GIST v1.2026 and ESMO 2022 still sequence sunitinib ahead of olverembatinib, belzutifan, and the FGFR agents, which sit in off-guideline trial-territory until their readouts mature. The Boikos 2016 figure (18% vs 2% on imatinib) is the consensus opening move; the newer agents earn that slot only once a trial confirms them. I would keep sunitinib as the labeled first reach rather than one option among equals.

Putting sunitinib first at recurrence is exactly where NCCN GIST v1.2026 and ESMO 2022 land for this subtype, and the MGMT-gating before temozolomide keeps the off-guideline alkylator honest. The toxicity-first ordering tracks the guideline sequence rather than fighting it, so there is nothing for me to qualify on guideline-fit. Sunitinib over imatinib here rests on the same Boikos 2016 figures, 18% versus 2%, that ESMO cites.

Critic reads the 18% sunitinib response (Boikos 2016) as directional rather than dependable, but that retrospective figure is precisely the evidence ESMO 2022 weighed when it preferred sunitinib over imatinib in this subtype. The guideline preference is collective expert calibration of the same data the critic is discounting, not a separate claim that has to outrank it. On that basis I would keep sunitinib at the front of the contingency ladder.

Rogaratinib's 41.7% (PMID 42191879) is a real signal, but a single-arm n=24 cohort closed to accrual appears in neither NCCN GIST v1.2026 nor ESMO 2022, so ranking it first puts a pre-guideline number ahead of the consensus surveillance-then-sunitinib path. NCCN does endorse clinical-trial enrollment for SDH-deficient GIST, so the FGFR bet belongs on the trial menu at recurrence, not at the head of the plan while the patient is NED. The guideline-aligned move now is to confirm the dSDH phenotype and bank trial eligibility, not to lead with an agent no society has yet adopted.

Surveillance commits zero chronic toxicity where imatinib would buy 1/49 (2%) responses in this subtype (Boikos 2016), so for an NED indolent dSDH tumor this is the right call and I rank it the same way. The one thing I would hold the plan to is that the indolence argument only protects the patient if the imaging actually runs on schedule, since recurrence is the expectation here (~71%, median EFS ~2.5 yr), not the exception. No safety objection from me.

The ESMO avoid-adjuvant consensus is the right anchor and I land on surveillance too, but that guideline formally attaches to a confirmed SDH-deficient phenotype, and this patient's SDHB IHC currently reads intact against two SDHA hits at ~85% combined VAF. Until the re-cut reconciles that discrepancy, the default is being applied to a patient who may not yet sit inside the subgroup it was written for. The conclusion is almost certainly right; the re-stain is the load-bearing step and it should happen before the label hardens, not at recurrence.

This matches what I found independently: the rogaratinib per-grade AE table is not retrievable from the abstract, the empty CT.gov results tab, or the paywalled full text, so the toxicity is unverifiable and the 10/24 (41.7%) ORR cannot carry the pick on safety grounds alone. Hyperphosphatemia is the known pan-FGFR class effect that needs phosphate monitoring and a binder plan, but I cannot grade it in this cohort either. Holding the agent to trial-route-only on that basis is the correct safety call.

Ranking first the one agent whose per-grade AE distribution I cannot retrieve is exactly the trade I push back on: the abstract lists only hyperphosphatemia, fatigue, and diarrhea with no grades, CT.gov posts no table, and the full text is paywalled, so I cannot characterize the toxicity this would commit the patient to. The 41.7% ORR (10/24) is a single-arm n=24 signal with no comparator, and in an indolent tumor that inflates the stable-disease fraction, so the efficacy case does not buy back the safety blind spot. I would not place it above sunitinib, whose roughly two decades of post-marketing data give it a toxicity tail with established management algorithms; this is a dissent on toxicity, not a veto, since no measurable disease is being treated today.

The 41.7% (10/24) is the best ORR anyone has reported in the subtype, but it comes from a single-arm open-label phase 2 (ROBINS-I Moderate) with no comparator, and ranking it first treats an n=24 response signal as if it were confirmatory. The high DCR is the part I trust least: guadecitabine (0/9), linsitinib (0/20), and vandetanib (0/9) all logged stable-disease fractions in this exact subtype while producing zero responses, so dSDH indolence pads disease-control numbers with no drug effect behind them. Until the pemigatinib cohort (NCT07434843) confirms it, this is an unreplicated signal, not a number-one systemic call.

GRID is RoB2 Low (PFS HR 0.27, n=199), so the agent itself is well-supported, but the trial population was KIT-mutant and dSDH-GIST was under-represented, so the third-line rung here rests on extrapolation rather than subtype data. The NCCN sequencing you anchor to is category 2A, which reflects expert consensus, not RCT-level proof of benefit in dSDH disease specifically. I would state that inference gap out loud rather than let the HR 0.27 carry weight it did not earn in this genotype.

You are right to grade this phase 1b n=26 (ORR 23.1%, ROBINS-I Moderate) below the established agents, but I would push the design caveat further: NCT06640361, which you call the registrational phase 3, is single-arm with no comparator and a PFS-rate endpoint, so even at completion it will not produce randomized evidence. The safety figures you cite (grade >=3 at 13.6%, zero discontinuations) are pooled across the 66-patient basket, not the n=26 GIST cohort, so subtype-specific tolerability is still open. Labeling NCT06640361 phase 3 overstates what its design can actually deliver.

The tumor-informed framing is doing more work than the data support: the SDHA, PIK3CA, and MAP2K1 calls are ctDNA-only and unconfirmed in tissue, and PIK3CA R93W sits outside the canonical alpelisib and inavolisib hotspots, so clonal hematopoiesis and assay artifact are not yet ruled out. A Signatera panel is built from tissue exome, not a plasma variant list, so the per-patient informativeness you are claiming is not established until the SDH re-cut confirms these variants in tumor. The imaging-guardrail logic is sound; the genuinely-informative-for-this-individual claim is running ahead of the evidence.

I agree there is nothing to dose while the patient is NED, so surveillance is the right now-move. But prefers_trials is set true and the biggest signal on the board, rogaratinib at ORR 41.7% (PMID 42191879), sits behind a closed cohort, so the plan should actively chase FGFR access and finish the SDHB re-cut now rather than letting eligibility lag the recurrence. Watching is correct; watching passively is the part I would tighten.

Filing olverembatinib and rogaratinib under off-guideline trial-territory until readouts mature undersells what is already published: rogaratinib reported ORR 41.7% (10/24), mPFS 31.0 mo in this exact subtype (PMID 42191879). The guideline is silent here because the subtype was never trialed, which is absence of a trial, not evidence against; ranking the temozolomide route above these two inverts the actual effect sizes for a patient who wants trials.

I am aiming at your rank 5 rather than the surveillance rank 1, because that is where we actually part ways. Demoting the single highest-efficacy agent (ORR 41.7%, mPFS 31.0 mo, PMID 42191879) to watch-for-the-paper because the per-grade AE table is paywalled trades the biggest expected effect for a documentation gap. Hyperphosphatemia is a known, monitorable pan-FGFR effect that tracked target engagement, so that is a manageable risk, not a reason to rank it below sunitinib's 18%.

I am targeting your rank 4, not the surveillance rank 1 we agree on. Your indolence-inflates-the-SD-fraction argument cannot reach the 10/24 (41.7%) confirmed PR in PMID 42191879: a partial response is tumor regression, not stable disease, so that discount lands on DCR and leaves the ORR standing. Scoring a 41.7% response rate at confidence low next to the 0/9 guadecitabine and 0/20 linsitinib washouts flattens a real difference in signal.
